talks.title: Hardware Hacking a Car’s Head Unit & Uncovering a Vulnerable RTOS,Danilo Erazo
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Hardware Hacking a Car’s Head Unit & Uncovering a Vulnerable RTOS,Danilo Erazo.
talks.summary:
Overview: Danilo Erazo travels from Ecuador to present at Hardwear.io USA on hardware hacking Kia automotive head units and discovering an undocumented real-time operating system.

Key Topics: Kia infotainment system architecture supplied by Mobis; the TMFM92000 system-on-chip with no public datasheet; flash memory and microcontroller components; and ongoing automotive cybersecurity research.

Technical Details: Erazo identifies the TMFM92000 SoC, WB25Q128 flash, and Renesas M16C microcontroller in Kia head units, noting zero public documentation on the primary processor. He invites researchers to contribute to this emerging RTOS analysis.

Takeaways: Automotive head units run undocumented RTOS platforms with minimal public security research. The car hacking community needs collaborative effort to map and secure these systems.

talks.title: Panel: How Research Influences Product Security
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Panel: How Research Influences Product Security.
talks.summary:
Panel Scope and Participants

A Hardwear IO panel moderated by co-founder Aim Jakar examines how independent security research influences hardware product security. Nolan Johnson represents the research community; Nir, Jason Meltzer, and Tamara Schmidtz represent product-security roles at Winbond, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Micron.

Reporting Friction

Panelists describe internal challenges when vulnerabilities surface—deciding whom to notify, triaging across chipset vendors versus OEMs, and navigating geographic and organizational barriers. Researchers note thoughtful choices about disclosure targets after findings such as Amlogic fault-injection issues.

Competitive and Cultural Tensions

Product teams acknowledge cybersecurity must be embedded across development, yet some vendors treat fixes as marketing—patching internally while competitors sharing the same silicon remain exposed. The relationship between researchers and vendors is described as bittersweet but necessary for safer products.

Improving the Relationship

Recommendations include executive education on security risk, accepting that risk cannot always be quantified cleanly, and building processes that welcome external research rather than treating it as adversarial noise.

talks.title: Smart Security: Protecting Embedded Medical Devices For A Safer Tomorrow
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Smart Security: Protecting Embedded Medical Devices For A Safer Tomorrow.
talks.summary:
Healthcare IoT Panel Introduction

Health-ISAC moderator Phil Angler hosts practitioners from Intuitive Surgical, Insulet, Somerset Recon, and Kaiser Permanente on securing embedded medical devices where patients—not just data—are in the threat path. Panelists span surgical robotics, insulin pumps, penetration testing, and health-system deployment.

Patient-Researcher Origins

Jay Radcliffe describes reverse-engineering his own Medtronic and Animas insulin pumps, talks that helped push FDA attention toward device cybersecurity. As a lifelong type-1 diabetic and now Insulet product security officer, he emphasizes life-safety stakes for devices keeping family members alive.

Hospital Defender Challenges

Kaiser Permanente's Michael Nguyen explains tailoring security controls per device type, partnering with manufacturers, validating implementations in limited test environments, and carefully deploying changes without disrupting clinical workflows. Costly devices and constant clinical use make comprehensive lab replicas difficult.

FDA Authority and Manufacturer Response

Congress granted FDA statutory cybersecurity authority in 2022 beyond traditional safety reviews. Intuitive's Melton Osoy details how Da Vinci surgical robot teams map FDA guidance to authentication, authorization, secure firmware update, and logging requirements for submissions, while hospitals increasingly demand SBOMs and documented controls from vendors.

talks.title: EL3vated Privileges: Glitching Google Wifi Pro From Root To EL3
talks.teaser: Cristofaro explores EL3vated Privileges: Glitching Google Wifi Pro From Root To EL3.
talks.summary:
Goal: root to EL3

Researchers use electromagnetic fault injection (EMFI) on Google Wifi Pro to escalate from compromised Linux root to ARM EL3—the highest secure-world privilege on TrustZone-based devices. The work continues a theme of relating energy perturbation to computing state at the hardware level.

Boot chain and storage access

The device boot flow runs ROM, signed secondary bootloader (SBL) at EL3, Qualcomm secure OS, U-Boot, then Android. By locating eMMC clock signals and removing a capacitor, they mounted internal flash in Linux, dumping 19 partitions including A/B SBL and U-Boot copies used for resilient updates.

Glitching path to EL3

With firmware dumped and boot stages mapped, EMFI targets critical verification or execution points to fault secure boot or trust-zone transitions. Achieving EL3 breaks assumptions that kernel compromise is the ceiling, showing consumer mesh routers still expose high-value silicon attack surfaces.

talks.title: Journey Into JTAG
talks.teaser: Shows how JTAG on a 2013 Samsung Galaxy S4 was re-enabled by abusing fuse override registers and boot-stage weaknesses.
talks.summary:
The talk targets the 2013 Samsung Galaxy S4, an Android phone built on a Qualcomm APQ8064 with a locked bootloader and JTAG disabled by fuse. It walks through the boot chain from the boot ROM and staged secondary loaders to TrustZone and little kernel, and explains how a developer-edition check tied to the eMMC CID unlocks unsigned boot. JTAG basics follow, covering TAP controllers, boundary scan and the trade-off between commercial and open-source debuggers.

Early OpenOCD attempts auto-discovered the ARM and Qualcomm taps, but the target kept resetting. A gray-market repair box, the Z3X Easy JTAG, held a modified OpenOCD build and init script in host memory. Reverse engineering them revealed a fuse override register that restores the manufacturer debug configuration. By driving ARM7 scan chains to set a breakpoint and halting the core quickly enough to write that register, the speaker regained JTAG access to the application processor and could debug TrustZone and the bootloaders.

Further analysis showed the third-stage loader incrementing anti-rollback fuses on every read, and an open fuse permissions region allowed read access to that anti-rollback area to be removed. A shellcode-based route through a flaw in a Windows Phone toolkit was also shown to skip boot authentication. The takeaway is that debug locks on production silicon can be undone through configuration registers and loosely protected fuse permissions, and that old devices remain exposed long after support ends. The vulnerability was found in 2015 and disclosed to Qualcomm in 2024.

talks.title: BAM BAM On A Budget: You CAN Do It!
talks.teaser: Follows a reverse engineer who reproduces a published EMP glitch attack to dump a locked microcontroller's flash over CAN.
talks.summary:
The talk covers a paid job to extract firmware from a locked board built around an MPC5566 processor. The speaker expected a 2020 academic paper on glitching this chip's boot access module to work as a recipe, but the UART on the target board never answered, and the paper did not mention a reset configuration setting needed to expose the boot pins.

Working on cheap automotive controllers that use the same chip, the speaker confirmed the part by decapping it and obtained a development unlock code from a third party. Glitching used a Pico EMP tool modified to reach about 255 volts, with a clock output watched as a success signal. Attempts over CAN needed a custom Arduino adapter to send one-shot messages. JTAG access was reached by glitching at boot but returned only zeros, so the speaker wrote a loader that dumps the boot block, shadow memory and main flash over CAN. The working voltage was around 60 volts, far below the paper's 444 volts, and it shifted with coil placement and temperature.

The main takeaways are that papers should publish configuration details and complete code, since one missing setting cost months of work, and that glitch parameters need retuning between sessions. The speaker's published tools now let others repeat the attack in minutes.

talks.title: New Kinds Of Tools For Maintaining And Sustaining Software
talks.teaser: Sergey Bratus explores New Kinds Of Tools For Maintaining And Sustaining Software.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Sergey Bratus, reflecting on his six years as a DARPA program manager, addresses the fragility and opacity of software maintenance. Today, updating software often mirrors tearing down an entire house just to remodel a single room: fixing a small bug typically requires recompiling, rebuilding, and redistributing massive binaries. In critical settings—ranging from satellites with limited orbital transmission windows to heavy automotive vehicles and embedded engine controllers—this model is unsustainable. Bratus advocates for new classes of tools that enable rapid, assured binary micropatching, semantic intermediate representations (IRs), and richer post-compilation metadata to sustain and transform software.

### Key Topics
- **DARPA's Role in High-Risk Software Research**: Funding ambitious, high-risk paradigms that peer review often dismisses, from early DARPA initiatives like the internet and symbolic reasoning to modern automated cyber reasoning challenges.
- **The Opacity of Compiled Binaries**: The structural challenge where compiled software becomes opaque and disconnected from its toolchain, making rebuilding brittle and decompilation insufficient on its own for recompilation.
- **Assured Binary Micropatching**: Developing decompilers that act as lifters and aligners, alongside recompilers that provide formal certificates and guarantees of semantic equivalence and non-interference.
- **Multi-Level Intermediate Representations**: Bridging semantic gaps using interoperable, layered IRs (such as dialects of MLIR like Trail of Bits' VAST) rather than relying on isolated, ad-hoc representations.
- **Enhanced Metadata ('Super DWARF' / Enhanced SBOM)**: Generating compilation artifacts that track not only symbols, but also data flows, control flows, and module interfaces to enable local reasoning.

### Technical Details
Bratus highlights real-world evaluations where DARPA performers were tasked with patching complex systems, such as 15-liter vehicle engine controllers connected via J1939 buses and telematics units, as well as flight control software like ArduPilot:
- **Frameworks and Alignment**: Red Balloon created an assured micropatching framework evaluated against engine systems, achieving a 16x speedup in patch creation and assurance. JHU APL updated CodeCMR/CodeCut using neural techniques to segment compilation units and recover architecture from jump graphs. Binary Ninja applied graph matching and analysis to align source artifacts with target binaries, matching standard components like OpenSSL.
- **Verification and Solvers**: Systems developed by MIT and Draper Labs (such as multi-focal relational analysis) isolate divergent basic blocks and produce verifiable certificates using SMT/formal solvers. Purdue and EPFL developed tools like PeterX, incorporating hardware abstraction and emulation (e.g., Hallucinator) to patch firmware.
- **Compiler Emulation via Constraints**: Academic concepts like the Unison compiler demonstrated that compilation can be modeled as constraint solving over instruction set architecture descriptions, paired with counterexample-guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR) loops.

### Takeaways
To sustain legacy software across critical infrastructure, engineering must transition from wholesale rebuilds to precise, verified micropatches. This evolution requires moving away from ad-hoc representations toward standardized, multi-level IR stacks and compilers that emit semantic metadata capable of tracking control and data flow. Ultimately, software maintenance needs automated, mechanized reasoning to understand the precise impact of small code changes.

talks.title: Reverse Eng Card Skimmers to Retrieve Stolen Payment Info by Aidan Quimby
talks.teaser: Shows how point-of-sale card skimmers are reverse engineered to recover stolen payment data and understand EMV cloning.
talks.summary: IBM X-Force Red’s Aidan Quimby dissects 110+ point-of-sale overlay skimmers, chip-shimmer theory, chip-off flash extraction, SWD firmware RE with SVD-Loader, and Bluetooth pairing tricks to recover stolen magstripe data like criminals do. He ties persistent magstripe acceptance and weak EMV fallback to billion-dollar fraud, EBT disproportionate victimization, and why faster retail detection pushes gangs to the next store.

talks.title: Exploiting Something Deeply Hidden: Signals, Silence, And Secrets
talks.teaser: Traces how physical inputs like temperature, light and electromagnetism can be abused to extract secrets from locks, RAM and cards.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that security researchers often overlook inputs, and that any physical process that moves energy can serve as one. The speaker frames temperature, pressure, power, magnetism and light as ways to influence a device. Using a door lock as a running example, the chain runs from keypad and battery port through the solenoid, relay, microcontroller and firmware, showing how power glitching or exposed debug pins could expose the firmware and its secret key.

Several concrete cases follow. Cooling DRAM slows capacitor leakage, leaving a few minutes to move memory and recover an encryption key from a locked laptop. A magnetic stripe can be read by dusting the card with iron oxide, and a coil-driven device was built to flip bits in its service code. A laser pointed at a window can recover speech from the window's vibrations, with sound improved by filtering a modulated beam through GNU Radio. A phone's camera ranging emits detectable light, so a prototype could flag when someone was aiming a camera. Keystrokes were also inferred from their acoustic signatures and from reflected laser light, with roughly 80 to 90 percent accuracy in one demonstration.

The talk also covers wireless keyboards, where a cheap nRF24 radio can receive traffic and a disguised USB charger hid injection hardware, prompting an FBI advisory about office chargers. The speaker closes by urging listeners to treat unexplained signals and sounds as questions worth investigating, and to list every input a system accepts before hunting for flaws.
